title: Branches and loops
objectives: Write conditionals and loops in C++.

screens.title: Reading a C++ loop
screens.question: Tap every close that adds 1 to `ups`.

hints.text: `i` runs 1, 2, 3, 4. Each turn compares `prices[i]` with the close before it.
Index 2 holds 101. What came the day before?
104 beats 100 and 106 beats 101. The others fell.

feedback.correct: Day 1 and day 3 beat the close before them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each close with its left-hand neighbour only.

byKey.first: You compared every close with the first one, 100. The loop compares `prices[i]` with `prices[i - 1]`, the day before.
byKey.c0: The loop starts at `i = 1`, so index 0 is never counted itself; it is only the day before index 1.
byKey.c2: 101 is below 104, the close before it, so that day fell.
byKey.c4: 103 is below 106, the close before it, so that day fell.

explain.text: The loop runs `i` from 1 while `i < 5`, adding 1 each turn with `++i`. Days 1 and 3 beat their neighbour, so `ups` ends at 2. Braces, not indentation, mark what is inside the loop and the `if`.

screens.prose: A backtest tracks the **drawdown**: the close's fall below its peak so far, as a fraction of that peak. Slide through the days and watch the running peak.
screens.question: What is the largest drawdown you see, in %?

hints.text: Stop on each day and read the caption. Which day is lowest against its peak?

feedback.correct: From the 110 peak down to 88 is a fall of 20%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide to day 4 and read the caption.

byKey.start: You measured from the first close, 100. Drawdown is measured from the highest close so far, 110.
byKey.first: That is the fall to day 2. Day 4 falls further below the same peak.

explain.text: The peak only ever moves up: 100, then 110, where it stays. Day 4 closes at 88, which is $(110 - 88) / 110 = 0.2$ below it. A loop keeps the running peak in one variable and the worst fall in another.

screens.title: The parts of a for loop
screens.prose:
A C++ `for` has three parts: a start `int i = 1`, a test `i < prices.size()` and a step `++i`. The test is checked before every turn; the step adds 1. `prices.size()` is the number of closes, here 6.

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i < prices.size(); ++i) { ... }
```
screens.question: How many times does the body run?

hints.text: List the values of `i` that pass the test.
`i` starts at index 1, not 0.
`i` is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; at 6 the test fails.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out each `i` until `i < 6` fails.

byKey.six: You counted every close. The loop starts at 1, so index 0 is skipped.
byKey.four: The test is `i < 6`, so 5 still passes. The loop stops only when `i` reaches 6.

explain.text: The test runs before each turn: 1 to 5 pass and 6 fails, so five turns. Starting at 1 gives every close a day before it. This is Python's `for i in range(1, len(prices))`.

screens.title: Counting up days
screens.prose: `const std::vector<double>&` hands the function the caller's closes to read, without copying them; level 2 explains it. Hidden tests include an empty vector and a single close.
screens.question: Write `count_up_days(prices)`: how many closes beat the close before them.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 6 hidden tests that call count_up_days; each must return exactly the expected count.

hints.text: Start the loop at index 1, as on the last screen.
Test 2 is empty. Does your loop run at all when `prices.size()` is 0?
`for (std::size_t i = 1; i < prices.size(); ++i)` with `if (prices[i] > prices[i - 1]) ++ups;`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: The empty vector broke it. With `i < prices.size() - 1`, 0 − 1 wraps, since `size()` is unsigned: about 4 billion here, 1.8 × 10¹⁹ on a 64-bit desk. Start at 1 and test `i < prices.size()` instead.
byKey.test-6: Three equal closes are not up days. Use `>`, not `>=`.
byKey.error: The program stopped. If the message says index out of bounds, your loop read past the last close: test `i < prices.size()`, not `<=`.

explain.text: Starting at 1 means every `prices[i - 1]` exists, and on an empty or one-close vector the loop never runs. `std::size_t` is the unsigned type `size()` returns, so comparing it with `i` needs no conversion.

screens.title: Maximum drawdown
screens.prose: Now the drawdown you slid through. `for (double p : prices)` visits each close in turn, like Python's `for p in prices`. Return the largest fall from a running peak as a positive fraction: 0.2 for 20%. No closes, or one close, means 0.
screens.question: Write `max_drawdown(prices)`.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 7 hidden tests that call max_drawdown. Each answer is accepted within a relative 1e-9 (a zero must be exactly 0).

hints.text: Two variables carry across the loop: the peak so far and the worst fall so far.
Update the peak before you measure today's fall.
Inside the loop: raise `peak` if `p` is higher, then `double fall = (peak - p) / peak;` and keep the larger of `fall` and `worst`.

feedback.correct: A running peak and a running worst: one pass.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-6: In `100, 80, 120, 60` the worst fall is from the new peak 120 down to 60: 0.5. If you got 0.4, your peak stayed at 100.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 should give 0.2: from 110 to 88. Measure each fall from the highest close so far, not from the first.
byKey.test-4: A fall from 100 to 90 is 0.1, a positive fraction. If you got −0.1, subtract the other way: `peak - p`.

explain.text: The peak only rises, so one variable holds it. Each close's fall is measured against it, and the worst fall is kept. With no closes the loop never runs and `worst` stays 0.

screens.title: A loop over input
screens.prose: A program reads how many numbers follow, then the numbers. Loop `n` times with `std::cin >>` inside. Print the sum as `std::cout` prints a `double`. When `n` is 0 the loop must never run.
screens.question: Complete the program so it prints the sum of the `n` numbers.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs your program 5 times with different input on std::cin and compares what it prints.

hints.text: You know how many numbers to read, so a counting `for` fits.
Read one number per turn into a fresh `double x`.
`for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { double x; std::cin >> x; total += x; }`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: The sum of 1.5, 2.25 and 3 is 6.75. If you got 9.75, you added `n` itself: it was already read before the loop.
byKey.test-2: With `n` = 0 the loop must not run, and the sum is 0.

explain.text: `for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)` runs exactly `n` times, and zero times when `n` is 0. `std::cin >>` does not care whether numbers sit on one line or many. The last test prints 0.3 because `std::cout` shows six significant digits.

screens.title: One step too far
screens.question: With these three closes, what happens?

options.text: It reads `prices[3]`, past the end: this app stops it, a normal build may read garbage

options.why: You read `<=` as `<`. The loop also runs with `i = 3`, and there is no `prices[3]`.
Only `prices.at(i)` checks the index and throws. `prices[i]` does no check of its own.
The compiler does not know how many closes there will be. This compiles cleanly.

hints.text: List the values of `i` for which `i <= 3` is true.
The valid indices are 0, 1 and 2.
`i` reaches 3, and `prices[3]` is one past the last close.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out every `i` the loop takes.

byKey.last: You read `<=` as `<`. With `<=`, `i` also takes 3, and `prices[3]` is past the end.

explain.text: Indices run from 0 to `size() - 1`, so the test must be `i < prices.size()`. This app's library checks `[]` and stops the program; a normal build reads whatever memory is there. Use a range-based `for` when you do not need the index.

screens.prose:
The loops you wrote, in one place.

```cpp
for (std::size_t i = 1; i < xs.size(); ++i)  // by index
for (double x : xs)            // each value
while (std::cin >> x) {      // until input ends
    if (x < 0) continue;       // skip to the next turn
    if (x > limit) break;      // leave the loop now
}
```

A variable declared in the `for` lives only inside it.
screens.question: After `for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i) { }` comes `std::cout << i;`. What happens?

options.text: It does not compile: `i` exists only inside the loop

options.why: That is Python, where the loop variable outlives the loop. In C++ `i` ends with the `for`.
4 is the last value the body saw, but `i` no longer exists after the loop.
`i` is not reset; it is gone. The compiler reports an undeclared name.

hints.text: Where was `i` declared?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. In C++ a name lives inside the braces where it was declared.

explain.text: `int i` is declared inside the `for`, so it ends with the loop and `i` is undeclared on the next line. Declare it before the loop if you need it afterwards.

screens.title: Fills by venue
screens.prose: Each of a day's fills arrives as a letter: `L` for the LSE, `C` for Cboe, `T` for Turquoise. Any other letter is another venue. A `switch` picks a `case` by value. Without `break`, a case runs on into the next one, and this starter has that bug.
screens.question: Fix and finish `fills_by_venue`: return the counts for LSE, Cboe, Turquoise and other, in that order.

widget.how: The first Check downloads the C++ compiler (about 26 MB) and compiles in 10 to 15 s. Later Checks take 1 to 3 s. Check runs 5 hidden tests that call fills_by_venue; each must return exactly the four expected counts.

hints.text: Run the starter on `L` in your head. Which counts go up?
Every `case` needs a `break` at its end.
Add `break;` after `++counts[0]`, a `case 'T':`, and `default: ++counts[3]; break;`.

feedback.correct: Each case ends with `break`, and `default` takes the rest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: `LLCT` should give 2, 1, 1, 0. If Cboe came out as 3, each `L` fell through into the `C` case: add `break;`.
byKey.test-3: `X` and `A` belong in the fourth count. A `default:` case catches every letter no other case names.

explain.text:
Without `break`, the `L` case ran on into the `C` case, so every LSE fill also counted as Cboe. `default` catches any letter no `case` names. Fall-through is legal C++, so the compiler stays silent unless you ask with `-Wimplicit-fallthrough`.

```cpp
case 'L': ++counts[0];          // falls into 'C'
case 'L': ++counts[0]; break;   // stops here
```

ideas: `for (std::size_t i = 1; i < xs.size(); ++i)` names a start, a test checked before each turn, and a step; `for (double x : xs)` visits each value.
Braces mark the body, and a variable declared in a loop ends with it.
A `switch` picks a `case` by value and falls through to the next case unless it hits `break`.

formula.name: Maximum drawdown
formula.note: One pass: keep the running peak and the worst fall.

summary.trap: `i <= prices.size()` runs one turn too many and reads past the end; the test is `i < prices.size()`.

options.why: You did the sum on paper. A `double` stores 0.1 and 0.2 slightly off, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004.
`==` compiles for doubles. It compares them exactly, which is the problem.

feedback.correct: The sum is a hair above 0.3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Are 0.1 and 0.2 stored exactly?

explain.text: C++ doubles behave like Python floats: `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance, such as `std::abs(a - b) < 1e-9`; `cpp-pricing` returns to this.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the values of `i`.

byKey.five: With `<=`, 5 also passes the test. `i` takes 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

explain.text: `i` runs 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: six values, because `<=` lets 5 through.

quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: `prices.size() - 1` wraps to a huge number, so the loop reads past the end
The loop never runs, because 0 − 1 is −1
options.why: `size()` returns an unsigned `std::size_t`, which cannot be −1. 0 − 1 wraps to its largest value.
The test `0 < 0 - 1` is the question. In unsigned arithmetic 0 − 1 is huge, so it is true many times.
It compiles cleanly. The compiler cannot know the vector will be empty when the loop runs.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What type does `size()` return?

explain.text: `size()` is a `std::size_t`, which has no negatives, so 0 − 1 wraps to its maximum. The loop then indexes an empty vector. Write `i + 1 < prices.size()` instead.

quiz.question: What is `day` at the end?

feedback.correct: 94.0 triggers the stop on the third close, before `++day`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `break` leaves the loop at once.

byKey.count: You counted the trigger day too. `break` runs before `++day` on that turn.
byKey.idx: `break` leaves the loop; the later closes are never visited.

explain.text: 101.0 and 97.5 pass and add 1 each. 94.0 is below 95, so `break` leaves the loop before `++day`. `day` is 2, the index of the close that triggered the stop.
